title: No room (Luke 2:1–7)
hook: a census, a long road, and a baby laid in an animal's feeding trough
carry: God arrived in a feeding trough

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joseph's dream: a just man who meant to leave quietly, and stayed.

Luke opens with an emperor far away signing an order: "And it came to pass in those days, that there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed." A census, so everyone can be taxed. Historians still argue about exactly which census Luke means. In a small town in Galilee, a carpenter has to pack up. Joseph belongs to David's family, so he goes south to Bethlehem, David's old town. And he takes Mary, who is, in the old words, great with child. No donkey is mentioned; Luke just says they went. And while they're there, the days are accomplished. The baby comes.
screen: `A DECREE FROM CAESAR AUGUSTUS.` → `A LONG ROAD SOUTH.` → `THE BABY COMES.`

segments.voice: Luke tells the birth in one sentence: "And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn." No star, no angels yet, no ox and no donkey. A manger is a feeding trough; Luke's Greek word is phatne. And there's a clue about the room. The word translated "inn" turns up later in Luke for the guest room where Jesus eats his last supper. So some scholars picture not a hotel with a rude innkeeper, but a crowded family house with the guest room already full, and the animals brought in at night to the lower part of the house, trough and all. Nobody knows for certain. The ox and the donkey come later, from Christians reading an old line in Isaiah: the ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master's crib. Crib, in that old English, means the manger. And near the end of his life, Bonaventure's life of him says, Francis of Assisi set up a manger with a real ox and donkey at Greccio, in Italy, so ordinary people could see it. Tradition traces the nativity scene back to that night. Some see the humility of God: the one they call the Word made flesh, laid where the animals eat. In Orthodox icons of the birth, the manger often looks like a small stone tomb, and the swaddling bands like grave cloths, a hint of how the story ends. The emperor gets the first line. The trough gets the baby.
screen: `ONE SENTENCE FOR THE BIRTH.` · `A MANGER IS A FEEDING TROUGH.` · `A FULL HOUSE, NOT A RUDE INN?` · `THE OX, THE DONKEY, AND FRANCIS.` · then, large: `GOD ARRIVED IN A FEEDING TROUGH.`

segments.voice: Think of your day as a house with every room already full: plans, errands, the people you expect. Picture one small space cleared for whatever turns up: a stranger's question, a child who wants to show you something, a slow conversation. If you pray, offer that space as a place for God; if you don't, just leave it empty, on purpose.
Manger. A feeding trough for animals, and, in Luke, the first bed Jesus had, because there was no room.
Your line: God arrived in a feeding trough. Of all the beds, that one. That's forty-one.

howItsDone: Many Christian homes and churches set up a nativity scene at Christmas, a custom often traced to Francis of Assisi at Greccio, and many churches read Luke 2 aloud on Christmas Eve.

what a scholar hears: Luke's word for the "inn," kataluma, is the same word he uses for the guest room of the last supper, so some picture a full family house, with the animals indoors at night.

notes: The index carry is 'God arrived in a feeding trough' (lowercase 'god'); the spoken line capitalizes God. The screen convention capitalizes God, so the index could read 'God arrived in a feeding trough'. Owner-approved index edit suggested.
Census of Quirinius (Luke 2:2): the dating is debated by historians; the script says so in one line and doesn't argue it.
Kataluma as 'guest room' (Luke 22:11) and the family-house reading are presented as what 'some scholars picture'; confirm.
Greccio 1223 and Francis's live ox and donkey: Bonaventure and Thomas of Celano; confirm wording 'in a cave in Italy'.
Orthodox nativity icon: manger shown as a tomb-like box and swaddling bands as grave cloths; confirm.
'Several days on foot' from Nazareth to Bethlehem (roughly 90 miles by common reckoning) is an estimate.

Second review (2026-10-01): 'the most powerful man in the world' now 'an emperor'; cut the unsourced 'several days on foot' (also used on day 38); the garbled 'phatne gives us a clue' sentence fixed (the clue is kataluma); the Greccio year and 'in a cave' removed from the voice and games and attributed to Bonaventure; 'that's where the nativity scenes on so many mantelpieces come from' now 'tradition traces'; 'for many' softened to 'some'. Keeper: Bonaventure dates Greccio three years before Francis's death (1223).
